citation: docs/mip/0008-panes-across-machines.md, section 2 (the merge) and "How it lands" (why nothing is written for a tab no window has written yet). No oracle sits above these: what the copies add up to is Muster's own policy, decided in that MIP.
why:
What a tab spanning machines looks like when each machine keeps its own copy of the tab's whole tree. Every daemon holding a part of the tab keeps every pane in it, with the other machines' panes as foreign leaves, and no daemon knows the others exist, so only a window sees every copy. These cases pin the four rules that turn the copies into one tree and say which copies to write back.

A tree is written `columns(a@laptop, x@devenv@0.5)`: each pane with the machine running it, and each split's share after its second child. A copy is written as its daemon's test harness writes one, `[a|~x@devenv 0.50]`, where `~x@devenv` is a pane this machine keeps in place without running. A write reads `devenv 2<-1 <copy>`: the machine, the generation it leaves the tab at, the generation it was worked out from, and the copy it sends. The cases with a change pin what a window writes when somebody rearranges such a tab: the change is worked out on the merged tree and every part that can take it is written one generation above the newest copy, since a part holding foreign leaves refuses a change asked of it alone (MIP-8, section 3). A change is written `ratio <turns> <ratio>`, `resize <pane> <side> [fraction]`, `swap <pane> <with>`, `zoom <pane>` or `even <pane> <scope>`.

cases.name: a tab no window has written is its parts side by side, and nothing is written
cases.why: Every tab grouped across two machines before this existed: each machine's part holds only its own panes, at generation zero. The window draws it as it always has, the parts as columns in the order its regions sit. Nothing is written back, because a part holding foreign leaves refuses the resize, zoom and swap that a window still sends one machine at a time, and that would break them in every grouped tab until a window sends those as whole trees.

cases.name: a tab arranged before keeps the widths somebody dragged its parts to
cases.why: The weights a window kept for its regions become the ratios of the columns, so a tab where the laptop's part was dragged to two thirds of the width still draws that way. Three parts make two splits: each split's share is its first part's weight over the weight of everything from there on.

cases.name: the copy a window wrote last wins, and a lagging copy is caught up at that generation
cases.why: The devenv was unreachable while somebody put x under a on the laptop, so its copy still has the older arrangement. The laptop's copy is newer, and the devenv is told the newer tree at the generation the laptop already holds: catching one machine up does not rewrite the others.

cases.name: copies at one generation that differ are settled the same way by every window
cases.why: Two copies at one generation differ only in panes their own machines added or removed, and the rules below reconcile those whichever copy is taken first. The tie still has to break the same way in every window, or two windows would write each other's arrangement back and forth. It breaks on the lowest pane id a copy holds of its own, which no window's config can rename. Both parts end up one generation on, so the next merge has a newest copy again.

cases.name: a pane is dropped once its own machine says it is gone
cases.why: x's shell exited on the devenv, which closed the devenv's part of the tab: its last pane there went. The devenv is connected and has finished restoring, and holds no x, so x leaves the tree and the laptop's copy is told.

cases.name: a pane on a machine that cannot say keeps its place
cases.why: The same copy, with the devenv unreachable. Only the machine running a pane can say it has gone; a machine that is not answering may well be running it still, so x keeps its place and nothing is written.

cases.name: a pane on a machine this window is not attached to keeps its place
cases.why: A second laptop's window attached only to the devenv sees a tab whose copy names the first laptop's panes. It cannot ask the first laptop anything, so it keeps those leaves in every tree it writes rather than deleting another person's arrangement.

cases.name: the machine holding a pane names it, whatever the copy called that machine
cases.why: The name in a foreign leaf is the one the writing window's config gives the machine, and another window may call the devenv `work`. The window finds a leaf's machine by asking which attached machine holds the pane, and uses the name only when none does. Both copies then hold the same tree, and nothing is written: writing this window's name back would have the other window write its own back in turn, each a generation higher, for as long as both are open.

cases.name: a pane made on its own machine goes beside its sibling there
cases.why: An agent on the devenv split x and made y below it, which the devenv does on its own without a window. The laptop's copy, taken first on the tie, does not name y, so y goes where the devenv's copy put it: below x, at the same share. Its place does not depend on which copy the merge started from.

cases.name: a pane with no sibling in the tree goes in as a column at the right, and an older machine is not written
cases.why: The gpu's daemon is older than spanning trees: its part is its own pane alone, at no generation, and nothing can be written to it. Its pane goes in where today's window would put a second machine's region, as a column at the right as wide as each pane would be as columns. Only the laptop, which can hold the tree, is told.

cases.name: a zoom on a pane that is gone fills nothing
cases.why: The tab was zoomed on x, and x has gone from the devenv. A zoom naming no pane would leave the window filling the tab with nothing, so it goes with the pane, in the tree and in the write.

cases.name: a zoom on another machine's pane is every copy's, and copies agreeing on it are left alone
cases.why: The tab is zoomed on x, the devenv's pane, and both copies say so: the zoom is part of the tree, so the laptop keeps it too though it does not run x. Every copy already holds the merged tree and its zoom, so nothing is written. A window that read the laptop's copy as unzoomed would find it differing from the merge on every pass and write it again each time, a generation higher.

cases.name: on a tie, a copy whose machine holds none of its panes yet does not win
cases.why: Both copies are at one generation, and the devenv, still restoring, has not said it holds x yet. A part holding none of its panes has no lowest pane to break the tie on, and it loses to one that has: otherwise every window would start from a copy chosen by which machine happened to be slow, and the laptop's 0.5 would give way to the devenv's 0.7.

cases.name: a divider moved in a tab spanning machines is written to every part, one above the newest copy
cases.why: Somebody dragged the line between the laptop's panes and the devenv's. Each part holds the whole tree, so the new ratio goes to both, as one tree each. The laptop's copy is the newest, at generation 2, and the devenv's lags at 1; the change leaves both at 3, each write naming the generation its own copy was at, so a part that moved on meanwhile refuses it rather than losing what it did.

cases.name: a divider is named by the turns down the tab's whole tree
cases.why: The path is read in the tree every machine's panes are drawn in, not in one machine's part of it: second-then-nothing from the root would be x, a pane, so the split between a and b is first from the root. The devenv does not run a or b and still gets the new ratio, since its copy keeps them in place.

cases.name: a divider that is not there is refused, and nothing is written
cases.why: first then first from the root is the pane a, so there is no split to move. A drag computed against a tree that has since changed shape lands here; writing nothing is what the next merge expects.

expect.refused: the tab's tree has no split at [First, First]

cases.name: a resize across machines moves the divider a daemon would have moved in its own tree
cases.why: b, on the laptop, grows to the right: the nearest split with b on its left is the column split between the laptop's panes and the devenv's, so that is the one that moves, by the share asked for. It is the rule a daemon applies to its own tree, shared with it, so a chord does the same in a tab on one machine and a tab across two.

cases.name: a resize with no divider on its axis is refused
cases.why: x fills the whole height of the tab, so there is nothing above or below it to move.

expect.refused: no split on that axis holds x, so there is no divider to move

cases.name: two panes trade places, and each keeps its machine
cases.why: Swapping a and b changes where each sits in the tree and nothing about which machine runs it, so every copy is told the exchange.

cases.name: a zoom on one machine's pane is written to every part
cases.why: The zoom is part of the tree, so the laptop records a zoom on x though it does not run x: a window that can reach only the laptop still knows what fills the tab.

cases.name: zooming the zoomed pane puts the tab back
cases.why: One key zooms and the same key unzooms, as it does in a tab on one machine.

cases.name: a part that cannot take a write is left to catch up later
cases.why: The devenv is still restoring, so only the laptop is written. Its copy is then the newest, and the devenv is caught up from it once it has finished, as any lagging part is.

cases.name: evening out a tab spanning machines evens every pane in it, whatever machine runs it
cases.why: Three panes, two on the laptop and one on the devenv, each end with a third of the tab: the column split gives the laptop's side two shares to the devenv's one.
